items.prompt: Which of these best describes what a vector is, in the linear-algebra sense used in this unit?
choices: Any array of numbers, regardless of whether they relate to each other
An ordered list of numbers that together describe one single thing, like a position or a color
A single number with a sign, like +5 or -3
A named variable in a programming language
items.explanation: A vector is specifically an ordered bundle of numbers that describes one thing together — a 2D position (x, y), an RGB color (r, g, b) — not just any loose array, and not a single scalar number.
items.reference:
Vector = bundle that moves together
(x, y) — a position
(r, g, b) — a color
(dx, dy) — a velocity

Why: A vector is an ordered list of numbers describing one thing together — order matters, and it is not just any loose array of numbers.

items.prompt: A game entity's velocity is stored as (dx, dy) = (3, -1). Why is this a vector rather than two unrelated numbers?
choices: Because dx and dy together describe one thing — the entity's motion — and their order matters
Because both numbers happen to be small
Because velocity is always measured in meters per second
It isn't a vector — only positions can be vectors
items.explanation: dx and dy only make sense together, as one bundle describing direction and speed of motion — swapping them, like swapping x and y in a position, would describe a different thing. That's exactly what makes it a vector rather than two independent scalars.
items.reference:
Vector = bundle that moves together
(x, y) — a position
(r, g, b) — a color
(dx, dy) — a velocity

Why: A vector is an ordered list of numbers describing one thing together — order matters, and it is not just any loose array of numbers.

items.prompt: Is (100, 0) the same vector as (0, 100)?
choices: Yes, since they contain the same two numbers
No — order matters, so they represent different things (e.g. different positions)
Yes, but only if both numbers are positive
There's no way to tell without more context
items.explanation: A vector's components are ordered — (100, 0) means 100 in the first slot (e.g. x) and 0 in the second (e.g. y), while (0, 100) reverses that. They contain the same numbers but represent different things, same as (x, y) vs (y, x).
items.reference:
Vector = bundle that moves together
(x, y) — a position
(r, g, b) — a color
(dx, dy) — a velocity

Why: A vector is an ordered list of numbers describing one thing together — order matters, and it is not just any loose array of numbers.

items.prompt: What does a matrix represent in this unit's terms?
choices: A single vector written sideways
A reusable transformation that can be applied to a vector, such as rotate or scale
A list of every vector ever used in a program
A type of loop in code
items.explanation: A matrix packages a transformation — rotate, scale, move, or a combination — so the same matrix can be applied to any vector, rather than writing that transformation's formula inline every time.

items.prompt: Why is representing 'rotate 45°' as a matrix more reusable than writing the rotation formula inline in the code that needs it?
choices: It isn't more reusable — inline formulas and matrices behave identically
The same matrix object can be applied to any vector, and combined with other matrices, without rewriting the formula each time
Matrices run faster than any other kind of code
Matrices can only be used once and must be recreated for every vector
items.explanation: Once 'rotate 45°' is a matrix, it's a reusable object: apply it to any vector, or multiply it with another matrix to build a combined transform — the formula itself is written exactly once.

items.prompt: In plain terms, what does the dot product of two vectors compute?
choices: The straight-line distance between their tips
Multiply matching components and add the results into a single number, measuring how much they point the same way
The bigger of the two vectors' lengths
Whether the two vectors have the same number of components
items.explanation: Dot product multiplies each pair of matching components and sums the results into one number — the basis for both magnitude (a vector dotted with itself) and similarity (how aligned two vectors' directions are).
items.reference:
Dot product
a·b = a.x·b.x + a.y·b.y
Positive → same-ish direction
Zero → perpendicular
Negative → opposite-ish direction

Why: Multiply matching components and add — the sign and size of the result signal how aligned two vectors' directions are.

items.prompt: What is the dot product of (3, 4) and (3, 4)?
items.explanation: 3×3 + 4×4 = 9 + 16 = 25 — multiply matching components, then add. Dotting a vector with itself like this is also exactly how magnitude/length is computed (the square root of this result).
items.reference:
Dot product
a·b = a.x·b.x + a.y·b.y
Positive → same-ish direction
Zero → perpendicular
Negative → opposite-ish direction

Why: Multiply matching components and add — the sign and size of the result signal how aligned two vectors' directions are.

items.prompt: Two vectors point in exactly the same direction. What does that imply about the sign of their dot product (assuming neither is the zero vector)?
choices: It must be negative
It must be zero
It must be positive
The sign is unrelated to direction
items.explanation: The dot product is largest and positive when two vectors point the same direction, zero when they're perpendicular, and negative when they point in substantially opposite directions — its sign is a direct signal of alignment.
items.reference:
Dot product
a·b = a.x·b.x + a.y·b.y
Positive → same-ish direction
Zero → perpendicular
Negative → opposite-ish direction

Why: Multiply matching components and add — the sign and size of the result signal how aligned two vectors' directions are.

items.prompt: Geometrically, what does adding two vectors represent?
choices: Multiplying their lengths together
Starting at the first vector's tip and walking the second vector's distance and direction from there
Finding the midpoint between them
Rotating the first vector by the second vector's angle
items.explanation: Vector addition is 'walk one, then walk the other from where you landed' — component-by-component addition matches this tip-to-tail geometric picture exactly.
Add matching components: 40+10=50, -20+5=-15, giving (50, -15).

items.prompt: Which of these is a real use of matrix-vector multiplication, per this unit?
choices: Applying a CSS/canvas rotate-and-scale transform to a shape's position
Converting a string to uppercase
Sorting a list of numbers
Checking whether a file exists on disk
items.explanation: Graphics transforms (CSS matrix(), canvas/WebGL transforms) are a direct real-world use of matrix-vector multiplication — a position vector transformed by a rotate/scale/move matrix.

items.prompt: In a recommendation system comparing two users' rating vectors, which linear-algebra operation is typically used to measure how similar their tastes are?
choices: Matrix multiplication
Dot product / cosine similarity
Vector subtraction only
Scalar addition
items.explanation: Cosine similarity (built from the dot product) is the standard way to compare two feature/rating vectors for directional similarity — exactly the recommendation-system use case named in this unit.

items.prompt: A weather app tracks temperature, humidity, and wind speed together as one reading per hour. Is this a reasonable candidate to represent as a vector?
choices: Yes — three related numbers describing one thing (one hour's conditions) together
No — vectors can only have exactly two components
No — only physical positions can be vectors
Yes, but only if all three numbers use the same unit
items.explanation: A vector doesn't need exactly two components, doesn't need to be a position, and doesn't need matching units — it just needs to be an ordered bundle of numbers describing one thing together, which three related weather readings for one hour are.

items.prompt: Using [[2,0],[0,2]] applied to (5, -3), what's the result?
items.explanation: Row 1: 2×5 + 0×-3 = 10. Row 2: 0×5 + 2×-3 = -6. Result (10, -6) — this matrix doubles both coordinates.
items.reference:
Matrix × vector
[a b] [x] [a·x + b·y]
[c d] [y] = [c·x + d·y]

Why: Each row of the matrix is dotted with the vector — the top row makes the new x, the bottom row makes the new y.

items.prompt: Matrix [[0,1],[1,0]] applied to vector (7, 2) — what does this particular matrix do?
choices: Doubles both coordinates
Swaps the x and y coordinates, giving (2, 7)
Leaves the vector unchanged
Negates both coordinates
items.explanation: Row 1: 0×7 + 1×2 = 2. Row 2: 1×7 + 0×2 = 7. Result (2, 7) — each row picks out the other component, so this matrix swaps x and y.
items.reference:
Matrix × vector
[a b] [x] [a·x + b·y]
[c d] [y] = [c·x + d·y]

Why: Each row of the matrix is dotted with the vector — the top row makes the new x, the bottom row makes the new y.

items.prompt: For a 2×2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]] applied to (x,y), which expression gives the new y-coordinate?
choices: a·x + b·y
c·x + d·y
a·x + c·y
b·y + d·x only
items.explanation: The new y-coordinate comes from dotting the matrix's bottom row (c, d) with the vector (x, y): c·x + d·y. The top row (a, b) produces the new x-coordinate instead.
items.reference:
Matrix × vector
[a b] [x] [a·x + b·y]
[c d] [y] = [c·x + d·y]

Why: Each row of the matrix is dotted with the vector — the top row makes the new x, the bottom row makes the new y.

items.prompt: For matrices in general, does A·B always equal B·A?
choices: Yes, matrix multiplication is always commutative, like ordinary number multiplication
No — matrix multiplication is not commutative in general; order can change the result
Only for 2×2 matrices
Only if both matrices represent rotations
items.explanation: Unlike ordinary number multiplication, A·B ≠ B·A in general for matrices — this unit's rotate-then-scale vs scale-then-rotate example showed two concretely different results from the same two matrices, just reordered.
items.reference:
A·B ≠ B·A (in general)
Rotate then scale ≠ Scale then rotate
(unless the two matrices happen to commute)

Why: Matrix multiplication bakes order into the arithmetic — reordering two transforms is only safe when those specific matrices commute, not as a general rule.

items.prompt: A teammate reorders 'rotate then scale' to 'scale then rotate' in an animation, calling it a harmless refactor. Per this unit, when is that reordering actually safe?
choices: Always — order never affects the result
Only when the two specific matrices involved happen to commute (e.g. a uniform scale with any rotation)
Never — reordering always changes the result
Only if the rotation angle is exactly 90°
items.explanation: Reordering two transforms is safe only when those specific matrices commute — a coincidence for some pairs (like uniform scale and rotation about the same origin) but not a general rule, since A·B ≠ B·A in general.
items.reference:
A·B ≠ B·A (in general)
Rotate then scale ≠ Scale then rotate
(unless the two matrices happen to commute)

Why: Matrix multiplication bakes order into the arithmetic — reordering two transforms is only safe when those specific matrices commute, not as a general rule.

items.prompt: Rotating v=(0,1) by 90° then scaling x by 2 gives a different result than scaling x by 2 then rotating by 90°. What does this demonstrate?
choices: A bug in the rotation formula
That order matters for combined matrix transforms — a concrete case of A·B ≠ B·A
That vectors can't be rotated and scaled in the same program
That 90° rotations are a special exception to normal matrix rules
items.explanation: This is exactly the non-uniform-scale example from L2: rotating first vs. scaling first land on different final vectors, a direct demonstration that these two operations' matrices don't commute.
items.reference:
A·B ≠ B·A (in general)
Rotate then scale ≠ Scale then rotate
(unless the two matrices happen to commute)

Why: Matrix multiplication bakes order into the arithmetic — reordering two transforms is only safe when those specific matrices commute, not as a general rule.

items.prompt: What does the identity matrix [[1,0],[0,1]] do when applied to any vector?
choices: Doubles it
Rotates it 90°
Returns the exact same vector unchanged
Returns the zero vector
items.explanation: The identity matrix plays the same role as the number 1 in ordinary multiplication — applying it to any vector returns that same vector unchanged.

items.prompt: Applying the identity matrix to (7, 3), what should the result be?
items.explanation: 1×7 + 0×3 = 7, and 0×7 + 1×3 = 3 — the identity matrix returns the vector unchanged, (7, 3).

items.prompt: The rotation matrix for angle θ is [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]. Where do the cos/sin terms come from?
choices: They're arbitrary constants chosen for convenience
They come directly from the geometry of turning a point on a circle by angle θ
They only apply to 3D rotations, not 2D
They represent the vector's magnitude
items.explanation: The rotation matrix's cos/sin entries come straight from the geometry of rotating a point around a circle by angle θ — the same trig used to describe circular motion generally.

items.prompt: What matrix represents 'rotate by 0°'?
choices: [[1,0],[0,1]] — the identity matrix, since cos 0°=1 and sin 0°=0
There's no matrix for a 0° rotation
items.explanation: Plug θ=0 into [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]: cos 0°=1 and sin 0°=0, giving [[1,0],[0,1]] — the identity matrix, which makes sense since 'rotate by nothing' should change nothing.

items.prompt: Why is it useful to compute A·B as a single combined matrix ahead of time, rather than applying B to v and then A to that result each time?
choices: It isn't useful — both approaches always cost the same
The combined matrix can be applied once per vector instead of two separate operations, and its order is fixed in the arithmetic itself
Combining matrices changes what transformation is being applied
Only vectors, not matrices, can be combined this way
items.explanation: Precomputing A·B collapses two operations into one matrix that can be applied to many vectors efficiently, and — just as importantly — bakes the intended order into the arithmetic so it can't be silently swapped later.

items.prompt: A·B·v is defined to mean:
choices: (A·B) applied first, then v subtracted
A·(B·v) — apply B to v first, then apply A to that result
B·(A·v) — apply A to v first, then apply B
It's ambiguous and depends on the programming language
items.explanation: Matrix-vector expressions associate so that the matrix closest to the vector is applied first: A·B·v means A·(B·v) — B transforms v first, then A transforms that result.

items.prompt: If A represents 'rotate' and B represents 'scale', what does the single combined matrix A·B do when applied to v?
choices: Scale first, then rotate — since B (closest to v) is applied first
Rotate first, then scale — since B (closest to v) is applied first
It represents neither operation, just a new unrelated transform
Rotate and scale simultaneously with no defined order
items.explanation: Since A·B·v = A·(B·v), B — the matrix closest to v — is applied first. With A=rotate and B=scale, scale happens first, then rotate, all captured in the single combined matrix A·B.

items.prompt: Implement `addVectors(a, b)` so it returns a new vector {x, y} equal to a + b (component-wise addition).
items.explanation: Vector addition is component-wise: add the x's together and the y's together separately, matching the tip-to-tail geometric picture from L1/L2.
items.reference:
addVectors(a, b)
return { x: a.x+b.x, y: a.y+b.y };

Why: Add matching components separately — the geometric "walk one, then the other" picture from L1.

items.prompt: Implement `addVectors(a, b)` so it works for negative components too, returning {x, y} equal to a + b.
items.explanation: Component-wise addition works the same regardless of sign — negative components add exactly like positive ones, no special-casing needed.
items.reference:
addVectors(a, b)
return { x: a.x+b.x, y: a.y+b.y };

Why: Add matching components separately — the geometric "walk one, then the other" picture from L1.

items.prompt: Implement `scaleVector(v, s)` so it multiplies both components of v by scalar s.
items.explanation: Scalar multiplication multiplies every component by the same number, stretching (or, for a negative s, flipping) the vector without changing which direction it points for positive s.

items.prompt: Implement `scaleVector(v, s)` and confirm it handles a negative scalar by flipping the vector's direction.
items.explanation: A negative scalar multiplies each component by a negative number, which flips the vector to point the opposite way while a positive scalar only stretches or shrinks it.

items.prompt: Implement `dotProduct(a, b)` returning the sum of matching components multiplied together.
items.explanation: Dot product multiplies matching components and sums them — here it also demonstrates that perpendicular vectors ((1,0) and (0,1)) dot to zero, matching L1's 'sign signals alignment' rule.
items.reference:
dotProduct(a, b)
return a.x*b.x + a.y*b.y;

Why: Multiply matching components, sum the results — this same function is also the base of magnitude (dot with itself) and cosine similarity.

items.prompt: Implement `dotProduct` and use it to build `magnitude(v)` — the square root of a vector dotted with itself.
items.explanation: magnitude is just the dot product of a vector with itself, square-rooted — the Pythagorean theorem expressed through the dot product, exactly as this level's text derives it.
items.reference:
dotProduct(a, b)
return a.x*b.x + a.y*b.y;

Why: Multiply matching components, sum the results — this same function is also the base of magnitude (dot with itself) and cosine similarity.

items.prompt: Implement `dotProduct(a, b)` and verify two vectors pointing in opposite directions give a negative result.

tests.description: opposite-direction vectors dot to a negative number

items.explanation: Opposite-direction vectors dot to a negative number — (1,0)·(−1,0) = −1 — matching L1's rule that the dot product's sign signals alignment: positive for same-direction, zero for perpendicular, negative for opposing.
items.reference:
dotProduct(a, b)
return a.x*b.x + a.y*b.y;

Why: Multiply matching components, sum the results — this same function is also the base of magnitude (dot with itself) and cosine similarity.

items.prompt: Implement `multiplyMatrices(a, b)` for 2×2 matrices given as [[a00,a01],[a10,a11]], returning their product a·b in the same nested-array shape.
items.explanation: Each entry of the product is a dot product of a row from the first matrix with a column from the second — multiplying by the identity leaves the other matrix unchanged, and applying the swap matrix twice undoes itself, landing back at the identity.

items.prompt: Implement `multiplyMatrices(a, b)` and confirm combining scaleMatrix(2) with itself gives a matrix that scales by 4.
items.explanation: Combining scaleMatrix(2) with itself gives scaleMatrix(4) — applying 'double' twice is the same as 'quadruple' — and combining any matrix with the identity leaves it unchanged, both direct checks on the row/column dot-product formula.

items.prompt: Implement `applyMatrix(matrix, v)` — apply a 2×2 matrix (as [[row1],[row2]]) to vector v, returning the new {x, y}.

tests.description: rotating (1,0) by 0 degrees leaves it unchanged

items.explanation: Each output coordinate is a dot product of one matrix row with the vector — the top row produces the new x, the bottom row produces the new y, exactly the row-by-row rule from L2 made runnable.
items.reference:
applyMatrix(matrix, v)
x = row1[0]*v.x + row1[1]*v.y
y = row2[0]*v.x + row2[1]*v.y

Why: The same row-by-row dot product works for any 2×2 matrix — rotation, scale, or otherwise — which is exactly why matrices are reusable.

items.prompt: Implement `applyMatrix(matrix, v)` and confirm rotating (0,1) by 90 degrees points it toward -x, and by 180 degrees points it toward -y.
items.explanation: Each output coordinate is a dot product of one matrix row with the vector — successive 90° rotations sweep (0,1) through (-1,0), (0,-1), and back around, exactly matching a quarter-turn each time.
items.reference:
applyMatrix(matrix, v)
x = row1[0]*v.x + row1[1]*v.y
y = row2[0]*v.x + row2[1]*v.y

Why: The same row-by-row dot product works for any 2×2 matrix — rotation, scale, or otherwise — which is exactly why matrices are reusable.

items.prompt: Implement `applyMatrix(matrix, v)` and use it with a scale matrix (not rotation) to confirm the same function works for any 2×2 matrix, not just rotations.
items.explanation: applyMatrix is generic — it doesn't know or care whether the matrix represents a rotation, a scale, or any other linear transform; the row-by-row dot product formula is identical either way, which is exactly why matrices are a reusable representation per L1.
items.reference:
applyMatrix(matrix, v)
x = row1[0]*v.x + row1[1]*v.y
y = row2[0]*v.x + row2[1]*v.y

Why: The same row-by-row dot product works for any 2×2 matrix — rotation, scale, or otherwise — which is exactly why matrices are reusable.

items.prompt: Two users' rating vectors are (5,4) and (4,3.2) — one rates everything about 20% lower but in the same proportions. What should cosine similarity report, and why?
choices: Close to 1 — cosine similarity measures direction, not magnitude, so proportionally-scaled ratings point the same way
Close to 0 — the raw numbers are different, so the vectors are unrelated
Close to -1 — lower ratings imply opposite taste
It can't be computed unless both vectors have identical magnitudes
items.explanation: Cosine similarity normalizes by magnitude, so it only measures direction — two vectors that are scaled versions of each other (same proportions, different overall size) point in exactly the same direction and score close to 1.
items.reference:
Cosine similarity
cos(a,b) = dot(a,b) / (|a|·|b|)
Range: -1 (opposite) to 1 (same direction)

Why: Dividing by both magnitudes cancels out length, leaving a pure measure of direction — ideal for comparing ratings at different enthusiasm levels.

items.prompt: Why does cosine similarity divide the dot product by the product of both vectors' magnitudes, instead of using the raw dot product alone?
choices: To make the result always negative
To cancel out each vector's length, isolating pure direction so differently-scaled vectors can be compared fairly
Dividing by magnitude has no real effect on the result
Because the raw dot product is always larger than 1
items.explanation: The raw dot product grows with both vectors' lengths, so a longer vector would score 'more similar' just by being bigger. Dividing by both magnitudes cancels that out, leaving a pure measure of directional alignment between -1 and 1.
items.reference:
Cosine similarity
cos(a,b) = dot(a,b) / (|a|·|b|)
Range: -1 (opposite) to 1 (same direction)

Why: Dividing by both magnitudes cancels out length, leaving a pure measure of direction — ideal for comparing ratings at different enthusiasm levels.
